cards.title: Stay alert and discern
cards.body: The Christian life is a constant struggle, and Francis is direct that the devil is a real personal being and not a myth or a figure of speech. Our weapons are prayer, the Word of God, the Mass, Confession, works of charity and community. We also need discernment, the gift of telling what comes from the Holy Spirit from what does not. He asks everyone for a brief daily examination of conscience.

books.title: Orthodoxy
books.author: G. K. Chesterton
books.why: A witty, joyful account of how one man found that Christian belief fits the world like a key fits a lock.

cards.title: The world as a wonder
cards.body: Chesterton says he learned his first philosophy in the nursery, from fairy tales. They taught him that the world is startling and did not have to exist, and that gratitude is the right response even before we know whom to thank. The sun may rise each morning, he suggests, because God never tires of saying do it again, as a child does. To recover wonder at ordinary things is the start of faith.
cards.try: Choose one ordinary thing today (water from the tap, a child's face, the evening sky) and thank God for it as if for the first time.

cards.title: Reason alone can drive us mad
cards.body: Chesterton observes that the madman is not someone who has lost his reason. He is someone who has lost everything except his reason. His explanation of things is complete and logical, but it is as narrow as a small circle. A mind that accepts only what it can fully prove shrinks in the same way. Accepting mystery, he argues, is what keeps people sane: one thing left unexplained lights up everything else.

cards.title: Truth holds opposites together
cards.body: Critics accused Christianity of contradictory faults: too gloomy and too cheerful, too meek and too warlike. Chesterton concluded that it might be the one thing that is the right shape. The faith keeps apparent opposites and keeps both at full strength: man is God's chief creature, and man is a sinner; we hate the sin intensely and love the sinner without limit. The result is balance.

cards.title: Tradition gives the dead a vote
cards.body: Chesterton calls tradition the democracy of the dead. It means refusing to hand everything over to the small group of people who merely happen to be walking about today. Our ancestors lived, suffered and learned things, and to listen to them is ordinary humility. For a Catholic this is a reason to receive the faith, the liturgy and the wisdom of the saints with trust, as an inheritance.

cards.title: Love the world enough to change it
cards.body: Neither the optimist, who thinks all is well, nor the pessimist, who thinks all is hopeless, will mend anything. Chesterton says we must love the world as a loyal citizen loves his country: without conditions, and for that very reason wanting to reform it. Christianity gives both at once, a firm belief that creation is good and a clear view that it is fallen. That pairing drives real improvement.

cards.title: Orthodoxy is an adventure
cards.body: People imagine that holding to right belief is dull and safe. Chesterton pictures the Church as a chariot racing through the centuries, swerving to avoid one error and then another, when it would have been easy to fall. Keeping the whole truth is the daring thing. He ends by saying that joy is the great secret of the Christian: sorrow is real but passing, and gladness lies deeper.

books.title: Life of Christ
books.author: Fulton J. Sheen
books.why: Archbishop Sheen's best-known book tells the Gospel story with the cross at its centre from first page to last.

cards.title: The one who came to die
cards.body: Sheen points out that Jesus alone was announced beforehand, by prophets over centuries. He also notes a difference from every other great figure. Others came into the world to live; Jesus came into it to die. For others, death interrupted their work; for him it was the goal he called his hour. The shadow of the cross falls back over the crib, and the whole Gospel is read in its light.

cards.title: No Christ without the cross
cards.body: A theme Sheen sets out at the start is that Christ and his cross cannot be separated. The modern world would like a gentle teacher who asks for no sacrifice and saves from nothing, while harsh ideologies offer sacrifice and discipline without love or redemption. Neither can heal us. The real Jesus offers forgiveness and joy, and offers them through self-giving love that costs something.

cards.title: Three shortcuts refused
cards.body: Sheen reads the temptations in the desert (Matthew 4:1-11) as three attempts to turn Jesus from the cross. He could win followers by filling stomachs, by astonishing them with wonders, or by taking political power through compromise with evil. Each is a way to save without suffering. He refuses all three. The same shortcuts tempt us: comfort, show and power in place of faithful love.
cards.try: Notice today where you are choosing the comfortable shortcut over the loving thing, and choose the loving thing once.

cards.title: He leaves no middle position
cards.body: Jesus forgave sins, claimed authority over the Law and identified himself with God. Sheen argues that these claims rule out the popular view of him as merely a good moral teacher. A man who said such things would be either what he claimed or badly deluded or deceiving. The Gospels were written so that we would face that choice and answer as Peter did: you are the Christ (Matthew 16:16).

cards.title: The risen Lord keeps his wounds
cards.body: After the Resurrection Jesus shows the disciples his hands and side (John 20:20). Sheen dwells on this: the scars remain, now glorious, as the proof of love and the record of the battle won. There is no Easter Sunday that has not passed through a Good Friday. For the believer this gives hope in suffering. Wounds borne with Christ are not erased; they are transformed.

books.title: The Return of the Prodigal Son
books.author: Henri J. M. Nouwen
books.why: A priest's long meditation on Rembrandt's painting of the parable, in which every reader finds a place.

cards.title: A painting that became a mirror
cards.body: Nouwen, a Dutch priest and writer, was captivated by Rembrandt's painting of the father embracing his kneeling son (Luke 15:11-32). Over years of looking he found his own life in each figure. The book follows that journey. Its starting point is that the parable is not only about two brothers long ago. It asks each of us where we stand in the scene, and whether we will let ourselves be welcomed home.
cards.try: Read Luke 15:11-32 slowly today and ask: which of the three figures am I most like at present?

cards.title: The younger son: leaving home
cards.body: For Nouwen, home is the place where we hear the Father call us beloved. Leaving home means going deaf to that voice and searching for worth where it cannot be found: in success, approval, pleasure or power. The far country is anywhere we try to earn the love that is already given. The son's return begins when he remembers whose child he is, and he is embraced before his speech is finished.

cards.title: The elder son: lost while staying
cards.body: The elder brother never left, worked hard and obeyed, and yet he too is lost. His obedience has turned to resentment; he compares, complains and cannot join the feast. Nouwen admits this was the harder brother to recognise in himself. This lostness hides behind virtue, which makes it difficult to see and to cure. The way home for the elder son is trust and gratitude instead of keeping accounts.
cards.try: Catch one moment of resentment or comparison today and replace it with a spoken thank-you to God.

cards.title: The father: love that does not force
cards.body: The centre of the painting is the father, old and nearly blind, laying both hands on his son's shoulders. Nouwen sees there a God who lets his children go because love cannot compel, who waits and watches the road, and who goes out to both sons, the wasteful and the bitter. He asks no questions and wants no explanations. His one desire is to have his children at his table.

cards.title: Called to become the father
cards.body: Nouwen's last step surprised him: we are meant to do more than return as sons and daughters. We are to grow into the father, compassionate as our Father is compassionate (Luke 6:36). He names three ways there. Grief lets us weep over sin and suffering, forgiveness welcomes without conditions, and generosity gives oneself away. Christian maturity means becoming a home for others.

books.title: New Seeds of Contemplation
books.author: Thomas Merton
books.why: A Trappist monk's reflections on the inner life, showing contemplation as the flowering of ordinary faith.

cards.title: Seeds in every moment
cards.body: Merton begins with an image: every moment and every event of a person's life plants something in the soul. As the wind carries countless seeds, so each moment brings seeds of spiritual life from God. Most of them die, since we are not ready to receive them. The soil that welcomes them is freedom and love. To see daily events in this way turns interruptions and duties into possible gifts.

cards.title: The false self and the true self
cards.body: Each of us, Merton says, is shadowed by a false self: the person I want to be in my own eyes and the eyes of others, built from pleasures, honours and achievements, as if I could exist apart from God. That self is an illusion. My true self is the one God knows and loves, and it is hidden in him. For Merton, to become a saint and to become truly myself are the same task.
cards.try: Notice once today when you act to protect your image. Quietly let it go and do the honest thing.

cards.title: Contemplation is a gift, not a technique
cards.body: Contemplation, in Merton's account, is a vivid awareness that our life comes from God and that he is present within us. It is not a trance, not an escape from suffering or responsibility, and not something we can make happen by a method. God gives it. We can prepare by faith, silence and a simpler life, and then wait. Its usual clothing is the obscurity of faith, not special experiences.

cards.title: Solitude that unites
cards.body: Merton, who lived as a monk, insists that solitude is not a flight from people. The person who goes apart from dislike of others finds only a crowd of his own demons. True solitude deepens love: in God we discover that we are one with all his children. A few minutes of real silence each day, in the middle of family life, serve the same purpose. They return us to others with more to give.

cards.title: Humility and letting go
cards.body: The way to God passes through detachment, which means being free from clinging, and Merton extends this even to spiritual things: our reputation for goodness, our good feelings in prayer, our own plans for holiness. The proud person compares himself with everyone. The humble person is at peace, since he no longer needs to defend an image. Merton treats humility as the plain condition for joy.

books.title: Jesus of Nazareth: From the Baptism in the Jordan to the Transfiguration
books.author: Joseph Ratzinger (Pope Benedict XVI)
books.why: A great theologian's personal search for the face of Jesus in the Gospels, written for every thoughtful reader.

cards.title: The Jesus of the Gospels is the real Jesus
cards.body: Benedict wrote this book as his personal search for the face of the Lord, stating that it is not an act of official teaching and that readers are free to disagree. He values historical scholarship but shows its limits when it splits the Jesus of history from the Christ of faith. His conviction is that the figure the Gospels present is believable, historically sound and far more convincing than the reconstructions.

cards.title: At the Jordan, Jesus stands with sinners
cards.body: Why would the sinless one accept a baptism of repentance? Benedict sees in it Jesus's whole mission in advance. He steps into the place of sinners, takes their burden on his shoulders and goes down into the water as he will go down into death. The Father's voice names him the beloved Son. Our own baptism joins us to this descent and rising, and to the same voice.

cards.title: What did Jesus actually bring?
cards.body: Reflecting on the temptations in the desert, Benedict poses a blunt question. If Jesus did not bring world peace, bread for all or a better world, what did he bring? The answer is simple: he brought God. He made known the true face of the God of Israel, and with him the truth about where we come from and where we are going. The temptation in every age is to push God aside as secondary to more urgent things.
cards.try: Before your most urgent task today, give God the first five minutes.

cards.title: The Kingdom of God is God himself acting
cards.body: Jesus's central message was that the Kingdom of God is at hand. Benedict explains that this kingdom is not a territory, and not a social programme we construct. It means God's lordship, his living rule, and it has come near in the person of Jesus himself. Where he is received, God reigns. To pray thy kingdom come is to ask for a listening heart in which God's will sets the measure.

cards.title: The Beatitudes are a portrait of Jesus
cards.body: The Sermon on the Mount is the new Law given by one greater than Moses, who speaks with God's own authority. Benedict reads the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3-12) as a hidden portrait of Christ: he is the one who is poor, meek, pure of heart, a peacemaker, persecuted. So they are also a guide for disciples. They overturn worldly standards and promise joy in the midst of trouble.

cards.title: Praying the Our Father
cards.body: Benedict gives a full chapter to the Lord's Prayer, in which Jesus draws us into his own conversation with the Father. We say our, so no one prays it alone or only for himself. The petitions teach right order: God's name, kingdom and will first, then bread, forgiveness and protection. The more we pray it, he suggests, the more its words reshape our wishes into those of Jesus.

books.title: The Lamb's Supper
books.author: Scott Hahn
books.why: Shows how the Book of Revelation and the Mass explain each other, so that Sunday worship comes alive.

cards.title: The Mass is heaven on earth
cards.body: Hahn, a former Protestant minister, first attended Mass as an observer and was startled to hear the Bible everywhere in it, above all the Book of Revelation. His thesis follows the early Christians and the Church's teaching: the liturgy on earth is a sharing in the worship of heaven. When we go to Mass we do not merely think about heaven. In a real though veiled way, we are there.

cards.title: Jesus is the Lamb
cards.body: Revelation's favourite title for Jesus is the Lamb, used more than two dozen times. Hahn traces it to the Passover in Egypt, where a lamb's blood saved the people and its flesh had to be eaten (Exodus 12). Jesus is the true Passover Lamb, sacrificed once and now standing alive before the throne. This is what the priest proclaims when he holds up the Host and calls it the Lamb of God.

cards.title: Revelation follows the pattern of the Mass
cards.body: Read as worship, Revelation falls into two parts: the opening of the scroll, like the Liturgy of the Word, and the marriage supper of the Lamb, like the Liturgy of the Eucharist. Its details are familiar from church: an altar, robed ministers, lampstands, incense, the cry of Holy, Holy, Holy, the Alleluia and the great Amen. The Mass gives the key to this difficult book.
cards.try: At your next Mass or Holy Qurbana, listen for the Holy, Holy, Holy and remember that you are singing with the angels.

cards.title: A covenant makes a family
cards.body: Hahn's constant theme is covenant. A contract exchanges goods; a covenant, sworn with an oath, makes people family. God's covenants with Israel were sealed by sacrifice and a shared meal, and Jesus called the Eucharist the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20). Each Communion renews that family bond. Our Amen has the weight of an oath: a pledge to live as God's sons and daughters.

cards.title: Come knowing where you are
cards.body: If the Mass is heaven come down, we are never a small congregation. Angels and saints surround the altar, and Revelation shows their worship affecting what happens on earth. Hahn concludes that faithful worship is the Christian's strongest part in the struggle against evil. He advises preparing: read the readings beforehand, arrive early, and take part with attention.

books.title: Searching for and Maintaining Peace
books.author: Jacques Philippe
books.why: A small, much-loved book on keeping the heart at peace so that God can work in it.

cards.title: Peace lets God act
cards.body: Father Philippe begins with our helplessness: without God we can do nothing good (John 15:5). The most important thing, then, is to let him act, and for that the heart needs peace. He uses the image of a lake. When the surface is calm, it reflects the sun clearly; when it is stirred up, the image breaks. Keeping inner peace is not selfish comfort. It is the best help we can give to God's grace.

cards.title: Fight, but for the right goal
cards.body: The Christian life is a real combat, yet Philippe says we often fight on the wrong ground. If our aim is never to fail, we will lose heart quickly. A better goal is to keep peace and trust whatever happens, including our defeats. The devil's main strategy, he says, is to trouble and discourage us, since an agitated soul is easily led. Refusing to lose peace is itself a victory.

cards.title: Worry gives way to trust
cards.body: Much of our unrest comes from fear of lacking something: money, health, security, the good of our children. Philippe answers with Jesus's teaching on the birds and the lilies (Matthew 6:25-34). The Father knows what we need. Trust like this cannot be partial; holding back one area for ourselves keeps us anxious. We learn it by actually handing things over and finding, over time, that God is faithful.
cards.try: Name the worry that weighs most on you today and say: Father, I entrust this to you; I believe you will take care of it.

cards.title: Peace with your own faults
cards.body: Seeing our sins should make us sorry, but Philippe distinguishes two kinds of sorrow. One is anxious and bitter, and keeps us turned in on ourselves; it springs from hurt pride. The other is calm, trusts in mercy, and sets us on our feet at once. After a fall, he advises turning to God immediately, asking forgiveness, thanking him for his mercy, and going on. Confession completes this for serious sins.

cards.title: Patience with other people
cards.body: The faults of those around us can rob us of peace as much as our own. Philippe points out that God himself is patient with them and gives them time. We should want their good and work for it gently, but without the agitation that comes from wanting them changed at our pace and by our methods. Annoyance rarely improves anyone. A peaceful heart helps others more than an irritated one.

cards.title: Deciding without tormenting yourself
cards.body: When a decision is unclear, we should pray, reflect and seek advice. But God does not always show his will plainly, and Philippe warns against the perfectionism that fears every mistake. After honest effort we should decide and then be at peace, since the Lord looks at our good will more than at flawless results. In small matters he advises simply choosing what seems best without long deliberation.

books.title: Catholicism: A Journey to the Heart of the Faith
books.author: Robert Barron
books.why: A confident, attractive tour of what Catholics believe, told through Scripture, saints, art and places.

cards.title: God became one of us
cards.body: Barron starts with what he calls the great principle of Catholicism: the Incarnation, God becoming human in Jesus without ceasing to be God. From it he draws a key insight. God is not our rival. Since God could unite himself to a human nature without crushing it, the closer he comes, the more fully alive we become. God's glory and human flourishing are not in competition.

cards.title: Jesus forces a decision
cards.body: Barron stresses how strange and commanding Jesus is in the Gospels. He speaks and acts in the very person of the God of Israel: forgiving sins, claiming to be greater than the Temple, asking for a loyalty above family and life itself. Such a person cannot be filed away as one wise teacher among many. Either he is who he says, and deserves our whole life, or he is not to be followed at all.

cards.title: Beauty opens the door
cards.body: Barron leads readers through cathedrals, paintings, music and poetry, convinced that beauty is often the best first step towards faith. A beautiful thing attracts without arguing; then it prompts us to ask what makes it good, and at last what makes it true. He also notes the Catholic habit of holding things together: faith and reason, Scripture and Tradition, grace and nature.
cards.try: Spend five unhurried minutes today before a beautiful image, church or piece of sacred music, and let it lead you to prayer.

cards.title: The saints show the faith alive
cards.body: For Barron the best proof of Christianity is the saints. He presents several, among them St Therese of Lisieux, St Katharine Drexel, St Edith Stein and St Teresa of Kolkata. They are very different from one another and each is completely herself. Holiness does not flatten personality. Each saint shows one side of Christ's own life, and so we need many of them, as white light contains every colour.

cards.title: Worship and the life to come
cards.body: Barron presents the Mass as the place where everything in the faith meets: the gathered people, the word of God, and Christ's real presence in the Eucharist. He explains the last things in terms of love. Heaven is the fullness of love for God and neighbour. Hell is the freely chosen refusal of it. Purgatory is the painful, hopeful purifying of those who die in God's friendship.

books.title: Hymns on Paradise
books.author: St Ephrem the Syrian
books.why: Poems by the greatest teacher of the Syriac tradition, from which the Syro-Malabar Church draws its prayer.

cards.title: A teacher who sings
cards.body: St Ephrem, a deacon of Nisibis and Edessa and a Doctor of the Church, taught the faith through hymns sung by the people. In these fifteen poems he meditates on the Garden of Eden in Genesis. He approaches God's mysteries with wonder and praise, not with prying analysis, and he uses images and symbols where others use definitions. He counts himself a beggar hoping for crumbs at Paradise's edge.

cards.title: God clothes himself in our words
cards.body: Ephrem warns his hearers not to be misled when Scripture describes Paradise in earthly terms. God, out of love, puts on our language like a garment, since we could not otherwise approach what lies beyond us. The words are true and are to be treasured, but they point further than they say. The right response is gratitude for this stooping down, and a reverent refusal to imagine that we have God measured.

cards.title: The mountain of Paradise
cards.body: Ephrem pictures Paradise as a mountain higher than all others, with God's presence at the summit. He sees the same pattern in Noah's ark with its decks, in Mount Sinai and in the sanctuary. The Tree of Knowledge stands like a veil before the holy place. The blessed are received at the level their lives have prepared them for, and repentant sinners are welcomed within its bounds.

cards.title: The robe of glory, lost and restored
cards.body: A favourite image of Ephrem and the Syriac tradition is the robe of glory. Adam and Eve were clothed in light, and by sin they lost it and saw that they were naked. Christ came to find Adam and bring him back into the Garden clothed again. Christians receive that robe in baptism and are to keep it bright for the wedding feast. Sin is a loss of dignity, and salvation is its return.
cards.try: Recall your baptismal robe today, and ask Christ to restore whatever sin has dimmed in you.

cards.title: Free will and the testing of Adam
cards.body: Why was there a forbidden tree at all? Ephrem answers that God gave Adam a small commandment so that he could win his crown freely. Glory was meant as the reward of obedience. Had Adam waited, God would have given him the very thing he grasped at. The serpent offered a shortcut, and haste lost everything. God's commands are his way of giving us more than we would seize for ourselves.

cards.title: The thief, the body and the Church
cards.body: Ephrem rejoices that the repentant thief was promised Paradise (Luke 23:43): a single cry of faith opened what Adam had closed. He also teaches that soul and body belong together, so that our full joy awaits the resurrection of the body. And he sees the Church as already a likeness of Paradise on earth, where the fruit that gives life to all is gathered each day in the Eucharist.

books.title: Chavarul: Testament of a Loving Father
books.author: St Kuriakose Elias Chavara
books.why: A Kerala saint's letter of counsel to the families of his home parish, as practical now as when he wrote it.

cards.title: A good family is an image of heaven
cards.body: St Chavara, the Syro-Malabar priest who co-founded the CMI and CMC congregations, wrote this testament for the people of his native Kainakary. He begins with the family itself: a good Christian family is like heaven on earth. Its members, joined by blood and affection, live together in love, respect and obedience to their parents, at peace with God and with one another, each seeking salvation in their own state of life.

cards.title: Keep love and peace, avoid quarrels
cards.body: His first counsels are about charity at home and with neighbours. Family members should love one another and forgive each other's faults and shortcomings; one who does so finds peace here and reward hereafter. He warns firmly against carrying disputes to court, noting that lawsuits ruin families even when they are won. An honourable family, he says, is one that bears wrongs and forgives.
cards.try: Is there a quarrel in your family or neighbourhood? Take one step today towards forgiving or being reconciled.

cards.title: Work honestly and live within your means
cards.body: Chavara is plain about money. Each person should work according to his state of life, since idleness breeds vice. He advises against borrowing without real need, against display and costly celebrations beyond one's means, and against wealth gained by fraud, which does not last. He is strict on wages: labourers must be paid what is just, and without delay. To withhold wages is a grave sin before God.

cards.title: Count no day without a good deed
cards.body: Charity to those in need runs through the testament. Chavara teaches that a day on which we have done no good to anyone should not be counted among the days of our life. No one who comes asking for help should be sent away with empty hands, and we should give what we can. He also asks families to treat servants and workers with respect and to care for the sick and dying.
cards.try: Before the day ends, do one deliberate good deed for someone outside your household.

cards.title: Children are entrusted by God
cards.body: The second half addresses parents. Children are a treasure placed in their hands by God, to be given back to him. Parents should teach them to pray from the earliest years, send them to school, know who their friends are, and correct them with firmness and affection, without excessive harshness. When they are grown, they should be free to choose their state of life, marriage or religious vocation.

cards.title: Order the home around prayer
cards.body: Chavara wants the fear of God, a loving reverence for him, to be the family's real wealth. He asks for a regular timetable in the home: a fixed hour when all gather for evening prayer, early rising, attendance at the Holy Qurbana where possible, and Sundays and feasts kept holy. He recommends good books and warns against bad company. A house ordered in this way, he teaches, passes its faith on.

books.title: Mere Christianity
books.author: C. S. Lewis
books.why: The most widely read modern explanation of the beliefs that Christians of nearly all traditions hold in common.

cards.title: The law we know and break
cards.body: Lewis begins with quarrelling. When people argue, they appeal to a standard of fair play that they expect the other to know. Everyone has this sense of right and wrong, and no one keeps it fully. Lewis takes these two facts as the best clue to the meaning of the universe. Behind the moral law is Someone who cares about right conduct, and with whom we have put ourselves in the wrong.

cards.title: No room for a merely good teacher
cards.body: Lewis answers people who accept Jesus as a great moral teacher but not as God. A man who was only a man and claimed to forgive sins and to be the judge of the world would not be a great teacher. He would be either deranged or something worse. Lewis says Jesus did not leave the comfortable middle view open to us. We must decide for or against his claim to be Lord.

cards.title: Pride, the great sin
cards.body: The vice Lewis calls the centre of Christian morals is pride. It is competitive by nature: it takes no pleasure in having something, only in having more than the next person. It sets us against one another and against God, since a proud person always looks down and so cannot see what is above. The first step towards humility is to realise that one is proud. A truly humble person will simply seem interested in you.
cards.try: Today, in one conversation, ask about the other person and listen without turning the talk back to yourself.

cards.title: Charity is a matter of the will
cards.body: Christian love for our neighbour, Lewis explains, is not a warm emotion. It is a steady wishing and working for the other person's good. We cannot manufacture feelings, so his rule is not to worry whether we love someone. Act as if you did, and affection tends to follow. The same holds for loving God: do what you would do if you loved him, and trust him with the feelings.

cards.title: Faith holds on through changing moods
cards.body: Lewis describes faith as the art of holding on to what our reason has once accepted, in spite of changing moods. Feelings rise against belief now and then, without any new argument to support them. So faith must be fed daily, by prayer, reading and churchgoing, or it will drift away. He adds a deeper sense of faith: discovering our bankruptcy and leaving ourselves to Christ, who then enables real effort.

cards.title: God means to make us new
cards.body: Lewis warns that Christ will not settle for making us nicer. Give him an opening and he intends to remake the whole person into a son or daughter of God sharing his own life, and he will carry the work through whatever it costs. The Church exists to draw people into Christ in this way. The paradox is that those who give up themselves find their real selves; those who cling lose both.

books.title: The Screwtape Letters
books.author: C. S. Lewis
books.why: A senior devil's letters of advice to a junior tempter, which show how temptation works in everyday life.

cards.title: Seeing temptation from the other side
cards.body: Lewis imagines letters from Screwtape, an experienced devil, coaching his nephew on how to ruin one ordinary man. Everything is upside down: God is the Enemy, and the man's good is their defeat. The device lets us see our own habits as a tempter would. The key lesson is that he prefers small sins. The safest road to hell is gradual, a gentle slope with no sudden turns and no signposts.

cards.title: Keep him distracted
cards.body: Screwtape seldom needs to argue his patient out of belief. It is enough to keep him from thinking steadily about anything that matters: fill his mind with the day's noise, the newspaper, lunch, vague feelings in place of clear questions. Lewis wrote before smartphones existed, and the point has only sharpened since. Silence and attention are a protection, and endless trivial stimulation is a spiritual danger.
cards.try: Keep ten minutes of real silence today, with the phone in another room.

cards.title: Dry spells are part of God's plan
cards.body: Screwtape explains what he calls the law of undulation: humans live in time, so their fervour rises and falls. The tempter hopes the low points will convince the man his faith was just a mood. But God uses those troughs more than the peaks, since he wants free love and not dependence on feelings. What the devils fear most is a person who no longer feels God's presence and still obeys.

cards.title: Live in the present
cards.body: According to Screwtape, God wants people attending chiefly to two things: eternity, and the present moment, which is the point where time touches eternity. So the tempters push the mind into the future, where nearly all fear, greed and ambition live. To do today's duty, receive today's grace and bear today's cross is exactly what they try to prevent, by keeping us busy with imagined tomorrows.

cards.title: Charity starts with those nearest
cards.body: The man in the story lives with his mother, and Screwtape advises building up daily irritations between them: tones of voice, small habits, remarks taken the wrong way. Meanwhile the man can be kept praying loftily for her soul while ignoring her rheumatism. Lewis's point is that love is tested first at home, in small concrete acts, and that spirituality which skips them is an illusion.

cards.title: The trap inside humility
cards.body: When the man becomes humble, Screwtape recommends drawing his attention to it, so that he grows proud of his humility. He also promotes a false humility that consists in thinking poorly of one's talents. Real humility, the letters make clear, is self-forgetfulness: being able to rejoice in something done well whether I or another did it, and turning attention away from self towards God and neighbour.
